points.description: Purpose: both are a more efficient form of broadcasting than flooding, minimising duplicate packets in the network.

RPF check: the node uses its unicast routing table to test whether the packet from source S arrived over neighbour N, i.e. whether N is the next hop on its best route back to S. Only then is the packet accepted for forwarding.
RPF forwarding: if the check passes, the packet is forwarded to all adjacent nodes except N. Otherwise it is not forwarded.

RPB learning: each node monitors unicast traffic to learn which best paths it lies on, i.e. it sees unicast packets travelling between A and B (in either direction) and so knows it is part of that spanning tree.
RPB forwarding: packets are forwarded only on edges that belong to a spanning tree the node is part of, excluding the incoming link from N.

rubric.notes: Full marks need the purpose (fewer duplicates than flooding) and both mechanisms stated precisely: RPF uses the routing table to check the arrival neighbour N is on the best route back to S, then forwards to all other neighbours; RPB learns spanning-tree membership from monitored unicast traffic and forwards only on tree edges except the incoming link. Each point is all-or-nothing: a vague statement such as "it uses routing to avoid loops" without the check against the route to the source earns nothing for that point. A wrong detail, such as forwarding back over N, forwarding on all links in RPB, or describing learning from broadcast traffic, cancels the point it affects. No partial credit is given.
